title: Log-domain and projected Schur stress for increasing cutoff
question: Can log-domain Gibbs likelihoods and explicit projection off the sqrt(pi) constant mode extend the R-415 Schur stress to larger cutoffs without mistaking floating-point zero-mode drift for graph disconnection?

new_perspective.principle: Use scale-invariant log-domain conditional weights and compute the positive graph spectrum on the orthogonal complement of the exact sqrt(pi) constant mode. This separates a genuine coercive-gap stress from ill-conditioned normalization artifacts.
route: Reconstruct coordinate Gibbs masses by log-sum-exp over energy eigenvectors instead of forming an underflow-prone density matrix diagonal.
Construct every ordered conditional row from log-marginals, subtracting the parent log mass before exponentiation and normalization.
Form the intrinsic momentum conductance from the rescaled positive row and project the normalized graph operator away from sqrt(pi) before taking its first positive eigenvalue.
Recompute the R-406 harmonic/Schur coarse and residual gaps and check the conservative Schur gap below the projected full gap.

Stress volume-two cutoff dimensions through 32, both collar orientations and three inverse temperatures, while recording raw zero-mode residuals, probability dynamic range and any direct-density underflow.
Repeat the computation independently and use hostile tests for raw unprojected rejection, naive underflow, weight rescaling, wrong projection and nonpositive log rows.
new_perspective.qft_bridge: A stable high-cutoff stress is a prerequisite for deciding whether the Schur lower bound can be promoted to a common-core estimate. It does not create a uniform gap or replace the analytic Hamiltonian-domain argument.

finite_theorem.log_domain: For energy eigenpairs (E_n,v_n) and coordinate basis U, log pi_i is obtained from log-sum-exp of -beta(E_n-E_0)+log|U_in|^2, followed by a common normalization.
finite_theorem.scale_invariance: Multiplying all positive conditional weights by a common factor leaves the normalized intrinsic operator unchanged.
finite_theorem.constant_mode: For positive pi, W=D_pi^(-1/2)L D_pi^(-1/2) has constant vector sqrt(pi); the first eigenvalue of W restricted to its orthogonal complement is the positive graph gap.
finite_theorem.schur_comparison: The R-406 harmonic/Schur certificate kappa_S=half min(kappa_coarse,kappa_residual) is checked against the projected positive graph gap.
finite_theorem.scope: The stress is finite and numerical. It diagnoses conditioning and extends the cutoff table; it does not assert regulator-independent Schur coercivity.

lean_crosscheck.boundary: Lean checks only scalar positivity, scaling and projection bookkeeping; log-sum-exp, graph spectra, Schur matrices, cutoff stress and QFT limits remain executable/open analysis.

promotion_criteria: Show that projected Schur gaps and the split heat inputs admit source-, cutoff-, volume-, phase- and exhaustion-uniform lower/upper bounds on one Hamiltonian common core.
Replace numerical log-domain stabilization by an analytic positive-measure and conditional-marginal estimate compatible with the R-399 shell.
Transfer any surviving bound to the R-415 proper-time budget and only then revisit broken-sector GNS coercivity.
stop_conditions: If the projected or Schur gap collapses under the increasing-cutoff stress, retain the finite table and record the collapse without phasewise promotion.
If log-domain rows lose positivity or the scale-invariance check fails, stop the stress and repair the numerical representation before interpreting a gap.
A positive projected finite gap is not a common-core, uniform, GNS, physical-gap, continuum, C6, Sector-A or Pre-A theorem.
boundary: T0 claim-nonbearing finite log-domain/projected-Schur cutoff stress only. It proves no cutoff-, volume-, source-, phase- or exhaustion-uniform gap, common core, phase selection, OS/KMS/GNS reconstruction, mass gap, continuum, C6, Sector-A or Pre-A closure.
no_overclaim: Projection and log-domain reconstruction remove a diagnosed floating-point failure mode and extend the finite stress; they do not turn finite numerical persistence into regulator-independent coercivity.
